Do you have a definition of open data reuse in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify it.
column4:
Open data is the public information collected, created and maintained by public sector organizations and published in an open machine-readable format (CSV, RDF, XML, JSON, etc.), allowing re-use for commercial or non-commercial purposes.
Reuse of public sector information is the use also for commercial or non-commercial purposes other than the original purpose for which it was created within the powers or functions of a public sector organization. The provision of public sector information to a public sector organization in connection with the exercise of its powers or functions is not reuse within the meaning of Access to Public Information Act. (Article 2a, APIA).

The system for electronic budget payments (SEBRA) is a system for monitoring payments initiated by budget enterprises included in it and managing payments within pre-set limits. The implementation and improvement of SEBRA is a major component of the budget reform and, in particular, of the reform of the payment system for the budget sector, through which the following main goals are achieved:
- improvement of the budget payments and rationalization of the payment process by centralizing the monetary resource in BGN in the Bulgarian National Bank and decentralized management and control of the payments of the individual systems, through the relevant primary administrator;
- implementation of aggregated control and management of payments by setting a general limit for payments to the relevant budget appropriations, with a view to ensuring rhythmicity in the financing of state expenditures.
Achieved results:
- modernization, simplification and rationalization of cash management and budget execution;
- improving efficiency in the management of budgetary resources;
- limiting cash payments to the maximum extent;
- increasing fiscal transparency;
- improvement of fiscal discipline.

A good example of an NGO initiative that uses open data to solve migrant problems in Bulgaria is the Bulgarian Council on Refugees and Migrants (BCRM). This organization actively works on various projects aimed at the integration of refugees and migrants, while using data to improve the effectiveness of its programs.
One of BCRM's projects is the "National Integration Evaluation Mechanism" (NIEM), which is co-financed by the European Union. The project uses data to track and evaluate progress in the integration of refugees in Bulgaria, providing a basis for improving integration policies and practices at the national level ( BCRM-bg.org ) .
Another important initiative is the "Refugees and Migrants Information Bureau", which provides migrants and refugees with access to important information and services through the use of data collected and analyzed from various sources. This initiative facilitates access to legal aid, healthcare and social services, which significantly improves the living conditions of these groups ( BCRM-bg.org ) .
The organization "Multi Kulti Kolectiv" also works actively in this area with projects such as "Kitchen against xenophobia", where the use of open data and cultural initiatives helps to overcome prejudices and promote social integration ( NGO Norway ) .
These examples show how NGOs in Bulgaria are using open data to improve conditions for migrants and refugees, as well as to reduce social inequality and integrate minorities. For more information, you can visit the websites of these organizations, such as the Bulgarian Council on Refugees and Migrants and the Multi Kulti Collective .

Open data enables local authorities and NGOs to identify specific needs and problems in residential areas. For example, data on demographics, the number of homeless people, the condition of the building stock and more can help direct resources to where they are most needed.
Open data increases the transparency of housing management processes. Citizens can monitor how funds are allocated for housing projects and participate in the decision-making process. This reduces corruption and inefficiency.
By analyzing data on pollution, noise, access to green space and other factors that affect the quality of life, measures can be taken to improve conditions in residential areas. This includes landscaping projects, infrastructure improvements

The use of open data in Bulgaria has a significant impact on solving problems related to health and well-being. Open data improves transparency, facilitates access to information and supports research and informed decision-making. Here are some specific ways this is done:
Open data enables effective monitoring and management of health services. For example, the National Health Information System (NZIS) provides data on hospital workload, the availability of medical personnel and equipment, which supports the optimization of the health system .
 Data on the spread of diseases and epidemics allow health authorities to take timely and effective measures for prevention and control. During the COVID-19 pandemic, open data on incidence and vaccination status were key to informing the public and making decisions.
Open data is an important resource for health research and innovation. Universities and research institutes use this data to develop new treatment methods and health technologies. For example, healthcare digitization projects use data to create telemedicine services and other innovations 
Open data on socio-economic conditions such as unemployment, income and housing conditions help to identify the social determinants of health. This allows health authorities and NGOs to develop targeted programs to improve the health and well-being of vulnerable groups) .
Examples in practice:
1. National Health Information System (NZIS) : This system provides open data on health services and epidemiological indicators that are publicly available and can be used for research and management decision-making.
2. Future Health Project : Uses open data to develop health care innovations, such as telemedicine and digital health services, that improve access to health services and quality of care.
The use of open data in Bulgaria has a significant positive impact on the health and well-being of the population. It facilitates informed decision-making, supports scientific research and improves the efficiency of health services. Expanding access to such data and its continued use will lead to even better results in the future.

Teachers can use open data to create interactive lessons and learning materials. For example, the use of geographic data can be integrated into geography or history lessons by creating interactive maps or visualizations.
Students and academic communities can use open data to research public issues and inequalities. For example, analyzing health care data can help understand differences in access to health care in different regions of the country.
Providing open data can encourage innovation and entrepreneurship. Startup companies and software developers can use data to create new products and services that solve real problems in society.
Open data can be used to teach programming and data analysis. For example, students can study programming by analyzing climate or economic data, which helps them apply their skills to real-world problems.
Open data can be used to improve education management and decision-making. For example, the analysis of data on student achievement can help identify weak areas and introduce appropriate measures for improvement.
These are just a few examples of how open data can be used to improve education and skills in society in Bulgaria and elsewhere.
Here are some concrete examples of projects that use open data in Bulgaria:
1. "Open data in the classroom" - This project is an initiative of the Bulgarian Fund for Journalism and Open Knowledge Foundation Bulgaria. Its aim is to promote the use of open data in schools through trainings, teaching materials and educational games. The project provides resources and training for teachers and students on the topic of open data and its applications in the educational process.
2. "Open Sofia" - This is an online platform that provides access to various data about the city of Sofia. The platform collects and visualizes information about traffic, public spaces, cultural events and other aspects of city life. Using open data, Open Sofia aims to improve citizens' awareness and encourage their participation in city governance.
3. "Education without violence" - This project uses open data to analyze cases of violence in schools in Bulgaria. By collecting and analyzing data from various sources, the project seeks to identify problem areas and propose strategies to prevent violence in schools.
4. "Transport Portal of Sofia" - This project provides data on public transport in the city of Sofia, including information on routes, timetables, tariffs and others. The portal allows citizens to get up-to-date information on public transport and plan their journeys more efficiently.
These are just some of the examples of projects that use open data in Bulgaria. Each of them aims to improve citizens' awareness, encourage their participation in public life and contribute to solving societal problems through the use of data and technology

The strategic goals and priorities in the field of energy and climate of Bulgaria laid down in INPEC are as follows: Regarding the "Decarbonization" dimension, Bulgaria will make efforts to increase the share of energy from renewable sources in the gross final energy. consumption and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. On the recommendation of the EC, Bulgaria raised the level of ambition for the share of energy from renewable sources in the gross final energy consumption from 25% to 27.09%, thereby betting on achieving the calculated goal, according to Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 In support of this goal, Bulgaria will build additional capacities with an emphasis on wind and solar energy. Also, if necessary to achieve the set goals after 2025, it is possible to hold tenders for additional capacities for energy from renewable sources, tailored to market conditions. Biomass use is projected to increase in all sectors: electricity, heat and cooling, and transport. The anticipated changes in the transport sector will have a significant impact on the development of energy from renewable sources, as well as on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. More specifically, Bulgaria will promote the introduction and use of electric and hybrid vehicles in public and private transport, envisaging the creation of low-emission zones in major cities. Yes, the use of open data in Bulgaria can have an impact on the level of employment through several mechanisms:
Innovation and entrepreneurship: Open data provides opportunities for innovation and entrepreneurship by creating new products and services. Entrepreneurs can use open data to develop new applications, platforms or business models that create jobs and drive economic growth.
Transparency and management of resources: Open data can contribute to more efficient management of public resources and finances. This can lead to better management and allocation of resources, which can ultimately create new jobs or improve the conditions of existing ones.
Education and skills: Open data can be used to develop educational programs and initiatives to support the development of the skills and qualifications of the workforce. Providing accessible information and training in data processing and analysis can make it easier for people to retrain or develop new skills that are in demand in the labor market.
These mechanisms are just some of the ways in which the use of open data can affect the level of employment in Bulgaria. By creating a more innovative, transparent and educated community, open data can contribute to increasing jobs and improving economic development.
project "Providing digital skills training and creating an adult learning platform"
The main goal is to expand access and provide more opportunities for quality education using the possibilities of digital technologies. The development and implementation of a virtual online learning platform will provide flexible and affordable forms of learning such as online distance learning courses and electronic resources for self-study.
After the creation and implementation of the virtual e-learning platform under Component 1, all courses in an electronic environment for the training of unemployed and employed persons, organized within the framework of the active labor market policy and financed from the state budget and from the ESF+ under the "Development of human resources", will be held through it.
The virtual e-learning platform will be linked to the My Competence Competence Assessment Information System, which presents competency models describing the skills and competencies required to successfully perform key positions and tools, as well as databases and electronic registers relevant to the training of adults - the National Labor Market Database of the Employment Agency (EA), the Electronic Register of Vocational Training Centers of the National Agency for Vocational Education and Training (NAPEO), etc.
The Platform will also have access to the training providers, as well as control bodies (e.g. MTSP, AZ, NAPOO, employers, etc.). They will be able to monitor and control the implementation of the trainings in real time. At any moment during the training period, it will be possible to check the attendance of the trainees, the completion of the curriculum by days, the success rate through access to the exam materials and tests, access to the materials and questionnaires for the evaluation of the training, etc. In this way, compliance with the regulatory requirements for the organization of training and the quality of the conducted training will be monitored.
Total estimated financial resource - BGN 379,470,088.
Project implementation period – 54 months (2022-2026)
Expected results:
The digital learning platform to be fully functional;
To operate 760 digital clubs in which access to the training platform will be provided
Approximately 500,000 unemployed and employed persons have received basic and/or intermediate level digital skills training
Approximately 100,000 unemployed and employed persons have validated their basic and/or intermediate level knowledge of digital skills
